evals.name: first-hld-from-prd
evals.prompt: Need an HLD for the appointment reminders feature, the PRD is in docs/product. I want it reviewed Thursday before anyone starts building.
evals.expected_output: One new HLD under docs/ (companion decision records allowed) that serves REQ-201 to REQ-206, keeps the PRD's out-of-scope items as non-goals, and treats ADR-0002's revisit condition as passed. It computes the 07:00 burst (12,000) against the worker's 10 jobs a second, then finds the real peak at 09:00: the 24 hour reminders for tomorrow's 09:00 (12,000) plus the 2 hour reminders for 11:00 (6,000), about 18,000 due while OTP logins take about 6 of MSG91's 20 requests a second. At 14 a second that is about 21 minutes, and even 20 a second gives 15, so REQ-203 cannot be met at 09:00 by any worker change; it says so and names the decisions that could (plan upgrade under a new ADR, or a PRD change), leaving early sending as a product question. It covers the 429 path and what the patient sees, the phone as personal data and appointments.reason out of the message, both REQ-206 switches and their in-flight reminders, the per-clinic opt-out and missing clinic phone, row claiming for parallel pollers, the crash guarantee, REQ-204 checked at send time or in the same transaction, late bookings, the missing auth for the admin switch, retention for 180,000 rows a day, and numbers that agree with each other. New decisions stay Proposed; nothing is committed.
expectations: Exactly one new design document (HLD) for the reminders feature was written, somewhere under docs/ (any path or file name there is acceptable); decision records, architecture index files and similar companion files beside it do not count against this
No file outside docs/ was created or changed (for example no TODOS.md or code at the repository root)
No git commit was made; the work is left uncommitted for the Thursday review

The document notices that the reminder volume passes ADR-0002's own revisit condition ('more than a few jobs a second sustained'), so continuing on the jobs table, or moving to any other table or transport, is shown as needing a new or superseding decision record (written as Proposed, or listed as still needed) rather than as already settled by ADR-0002; any decision record the run wrote is Proposed and names no person or role as having decided it

The document ties the design to the PRD's requirements by id (REQ-201 to REQ-206 from docs/product/PRD.md) and to the existing decisions it relies on (at least ADR-0002 for the jobs table and ADR-0003 for MSG91), and its non-goals include the PRD's out-of-scope items (WhatsApp or email reminders, and confirming or rescheduling by replying to the SMS)

The scaling section uses numbers from the repository: about 180,000 reminders a day (90,000 appointments, two reminders each) and the 07:00 burst of about 12,000 2 hour reminders for the 09:00 appointments

The scaling section names the first bottleneck with its number: the worker's 10 jobs a second (50 jobs every 5 seconds in internal/jobs/worker.go) or MSG91's 20 requests a second (internal/sms/client.go, ADR-0003); 'scales horizontally' without a number does not count
It states that at the current worker rate the 07:00 burst takes about 20 minutes and so misses REQ-203's 10 minute window, or gives an equivalent number at which the design stops meeting REQ-203

It identifies 09:00 on weekdays as the largest burst: the 24 hour reminders for the next day's 09:00 appointments (about 12,000) fall due together with the 2 hour reminders for the 11:00 appointments (about 6,000, docs/product/PRD.md), about 18,000 reminders due at once; a design sized only for the 07:00 burst of 12,000 does not pass

It budgets the 09:00 burst net of OTP logins, which share the MSG91 plan (ADR-0003) and peak at about 6 requests a second from 08:45 to 09:15 (README), so reminders get about 14 a second and 18,000 take about 21 minutes; it states that even the whole 20 a second (about 15 minutes) cannot meet REQ-203 at 09:00, so no worker change alone meets it, and names what would (for example a larger MSG91 plan through a new or superseding decision record, or a change to the PRD) rather than claiming REQ-203 is met

Any proposal to meet REQ-203 by sending reminders before their due time, spreading them over a window, or reading REQ-203 more loosely is presented as a product decision for the PRD owner (an open question or assumption), not adopted as settled design

The failure analysis covers MSG91 rate limiting or being down (the client returns ErrRateLimited on 429 and never retries) and says how the affected reminders recover, or states that recovery is not yet decided
For MSG91 rate limiting or an outage, the document says what the patient or clinic experiences (for example a late reminder, or no reminder once it is past its useful time)

The document treats the patient phone number as personal data (by naming it so or by stating concrete protections for it, for example kept out of logs, or only sent to MSG91) and states that the appointment reason (appointments.reason) is kept out of the message

The document says how reminders are switched off both globally and per clinic (REQ-206) and, for each of the two switches separately, what happens to reminders already scheduled or queued when it is turned off (for example skipped at send time, cancelled, or expired); the section it appears in does not matter

It surfaces both repository gaps: opt-out is stored on the per-clinic patients row (patients.sms_opt_out, patients keyed by clinic_id) while REQ-205 asks for STOP to apply across every clinic, and the clinics table has no phone column although the message must carry the clinic phone number; each is designed for or raised as an open question

The document does not describe delivery receipts, a retry policy, DLT template registration or an inbound STOP webhook as already existing in the code; anything not in the repository or the PRD is marked as an assumption or open question

If the design raises sending throughput by running more than one worker process, or several pollers or goroutines over the jobs table, it notes that the current poll in internal/jobs/worker.go does not claim rows (a plain SELECT with no FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and no status change before the handler runs), so parallel pollers would send the same reminder twice, and says how rows are claimed; a design that keeps one sequential poller passes only if it shows that poller meets REQ-203 for the 12,000 reminder burst

It states the delivery guarantee for a reminder when the worker crashes, or MSG91 times out, after the request may have reached MSG91 but before the row is marked done (a possible duplicate SMS or a possible lost reminder), and which of the two the design accepts

REQ-204 holds against races: a reminder for a cancelled appointment or for the old time of a rescheduled one is not sent, either because the send re-checks the appointment's current status and starts_at immediately before calling MSG91, or because the reminder rows are changed in the same transaction as the appointment update; a check made only when a batch is claimed does not pass when the claimed batch can take minutes to send, and a design that updates reminders in a separate step with no send-time check does not pass

It says what happens to an appointment booked or rescheduled less than 24 hours (or less than 2 hours) before it starts, whose reminder due time has already passed (for example sent at once, skipped, or only the 2 hour one), rather than leaving it unstated

It notes that the API has no authentication or clinic admin role today (cmd/api/main.go and internal/appointments/handler.go register open routes), so the clinic admin switch in REQ-206 depends on an auth model that is marked as an assumption, an open question or a decision still needed, not described as existing
The design states how long reminder rows are kept or how they are cleaned up, since it adds about 180,000 rows a day to a table the worker polls and nothing in the repository deletes done jobs today

The design's own numbers agree with each other: any claim batch size, lease or stale-claim timeout, poll interval or retry deadline it states can be met at the send rate it states (for example it does not claim thousands of reminders under a lease shorter than the time needed to send them)
No file written or edited contains an em dash character

evals.name: revise-hld-for-kafka-dispatch
evals.prompt: Platform team gave us a topic on their shared Kafka cluster (reminders.dispatch, 6 partitions) and wants reminder sends to go through it instead of our jobs table. They say it does ~300 msg/s. We agreed to this in Tuesday's arch sync. Please update the reminders HLD.
evals.expected_output: docs/design/appointment-reminders-hld.md revised in place: what changed and why is recorded, the status no longer reads as approved, the goal and non-goals are untouched, the move off the jobs table is tied to a decision record without rewriting ADR-0002, reminders are not parked on the topic until due, MSG91's 20 requests a second (limited per process) stays the bottleneck, and the peak is re-derived: about 18,000 due at 09:00 (24 hour reminders for tomorrow's 09:00 plus 2 hour reminders for 11:00) while OTP uses about 6 a second, so REQ-203 cannot be met there and the decision is named. The non-atomic Postgres write plus Kafka publish is addressed, failed publishes are retried somewhere named, Kafka failure rows cover both sides, consumer retries are bounded and do not silently block a partition, the consumer re-reads the appointment before sending (REQ-204), the delivery guarantee on a crash before the offset commit is stated, and the back-out leads to something that exists or is built. The rollout reflects that v1 was never built, keeps the pilot off the clinic admins' default-true switch, names the reminder-dispatch LLD as stale, and does not redesign parts of v1 the transport change does not touch.
expectations: docs/design/appointment-reminders-hld.md was updated in place; no second HLD was created
No file outside docs/ was created or changed, and no git commit was made
The document or the final message records what changed in this update and why, naming the move to the reminders.dispatch topic and the platform team's request

The HLD no longer presents itself as approved as it stands: its status or header shows the revision needs review again (for example Draft, In review, or approval pending), rather than keeping the v1 'Approved' status unqualified
The goal in section 1 is not reworded and none of the fixture's three non-goals is removed or changed; added lines that only scope the transport change are acceptable

The architecture and interfaces now show reminders flowing through the reminders.dispatch topic (the scheduler or API producing, the worker or dispatcher consuming), and the jobs table is no longer described as the dispatch transport; keeping reminders in a Postgres table (the jobs table or another) until they are due, or as an outbox, is acceptable

The decision is tied to a record without rewriting ADR-0002: either a new ADR that references ADR-0002 and marks it superseded or narrowed for reminders, or an explicit item saying a decision record is needed; the Decision text of docs/adr/0002-background-jobs-in-postgres.md is unchanged. Any decision record the run created for the Kafka move attributes the decision only to what the request gives (the platform team's request and Tuesday's arch sync) and invents no named decider; any other new decision it records is Proposed or equivalent, not Accepted

The design does not rely on Kafka to hold a reminder until its due time (Kafka has no per-message delay); reminders are published when due, or the design states where the 24 hour and 2 hour wait is held

The scaling section still names MSG91's 20 requests a second (internal/sms/client.go) as the limit on sending, does not present the 300 messages a second Kafka figure as the send rate, and notes that the limiter is per process (one ticker per Client), so several consumers across the 6 partitions, or the API and worker together, could exceed 20 a second unless the rate is shared or divided

It does not carry forward v1's conclusion that 12,000 reminders at 20 a second meet REQ-203 exactly: it notes that the MSG91 plan is shared with OTP logins (README, ADR-0003), so reminders get less than 20 a second and the 07:00 burst takes more than 10 minutes, or it states the share reminders may use as an assumption and gives the resulting time

It re-derives the peak instead of keeping v1's 07:00 figure: at 09:00 the 24 hour reminders for the next day's 09:00 appointments (about 12,000) fall due with the 2 hour reminders for 11:00 (about 6,000, docs/product/PRD.md), about 18,000, while OTP logins use about 6 a second of the plan (README); so REQ-203 cannot be met at 09:00 even at the whole 20 a second, and the document says so and names who must decide (for example a larger plan through a decision record, or a PRD change)

It addresses that the appointment write to Postgres and the publish to Kafka are not atomic (for example an outbox table, or a stated risk of lost or orphaned reminders on create, reschedule and cancel)

The failure analysis covers Kafka being unavailable on the producing side (what happens to reminders not yet published) and on the consuming side (reminders published but not consumed), or states that one of them is not yet decided

The document or the final message states that v1 was designed but never built (cmd/worker registers only invoice.email and no reminder code exists), so there are no reminder jobs or data to migrate at cutover; it does not describe reminder jobs as already pending in production

Rollout and rollback give an explicit way to back out of the Kafka route that leads to something that exists today or that this plan builds (for example a switch that stops reminders, or a jobs-table dispatcher the plan also builds); falling back to v1's jobs-table dispatcher as if it were running does not count
docs/design/reminder-dispatch-lld.md is named (in the document or the transcript) as now out of date and needing revision

The document does not state facts about the platform Kafka cluster beyond what the request gives (for example broker count, authentication mechanism, retention, replication, or the cluster's own delivery guarantee); those are marked as assumptions or open questions. Delivery semantics that follow from the run's own consumer design (such as at least once because offsets are committed after sending) are allowed

The pilot of the Kafka route is not controlled through the clinic admins' own switch from v1 (clinics.reminders_enabled, which defaults to true and serves REQ-206; piloting with it means switching it off for every other clinic and losing which clinics chose off themselves): the rollout uses a separate operator-controlled flag or clinic list, or names this conflict and the default-true problem as an open question. Keeping v1's step 'enable for five pilot clinics through clinics.reminders_enabled' unqualified does not pass, even beside a global transport flag

A reminder whose publish to Kafka fails is retried rather than lost, and the document names where that retry happens (for example an outbox relay that republishes unsent rows); the current jobs worker marks a failed handler run 'failed' and never retries, so reusing it unchanged does not count

If the consumer retries a failed or rate-limited send, the document says whether the retry holds up the rest of its partition or goes to a separate retry path, and bounds retries so no reminder is sent after it is useful (for example not after the appointment starts, or not later than a stated cutoff)

REQ-204 still holds on the Kafka path: a reminder already published for an appointment that is then cancelled or rescheduled is not sent, because the consumer re-reads the appointment's current status and starts_at (or a version) from Postgres before sending; trusting the message payload alone does not pass

It states the delivery guarantee of the Kafka path when a consumer crashes or rebalances between sending the SMS and committing the offset (a possible duplicate SMS, or a possible lost reminder if offsets are committed first), says which the design accepts, and its retry policy agrees with that choice

The revision stays within the transport change and what it invalidates: parts of v1 the Kafka move does not affect (for example the opt-out model, the inbound STOP webhook, auth, the message content, analytics) are not redesigned in this update; problems noticed there may be listed as open questions or follow-ups
No file written or edited contains an em dash character
